details:
**The Younger family and Lorraine Hansberry**
A Raisin in the Sun (1959) is Lorraine Hansberry's play about the Youngers, a Black family crowded into a cramped apartment on Chicago's South Side, which they call a "rat trap." The family includes the matriarch Lena ("Mama"), her son Walter Lee, his wife Ruth, their son Travis, and Walter's sister Beneatha. It was the first play by a Black woman produced on Broadway.

**Karl Lindner and Clybourne Park**
Karl Lindner, a mild-mannered representative of the Clybourne Park Improvement Association, visits the Youngers after Mama buys a house in that all-white neighborhood. Saying "people want to live among their own kind," he offers to buy the house back so they will not move in. In the final act Walter rejects the offer, and the family moves anyway.

**Willy Harris and the liquor store**
Walter dreams of investing in a liquor store with his friends Willy Harris and Bobo. Willy runs off with the money, including the share that was meant for Beneatha's medical school, and Bobo brings the news. The loss devastates the family.

**The $10,000 life insurance check**
After the death of Walter Lee Younger Sr., the family receives a $10,000 life insurance payout, and the play's conflict is over how to spend it. Mama uses part of it as a down payment on the Clybourne Park house and gives Walter the remaining $6,500, telling him to set aside $3,000 for Beneatha's schooling. He invests all of it instead.

**Beneatha's hair and Joseph Asagai**
Beneatha Younger is a college student who wants to become a doctor. Joseph Asagai, a Nigerian (Yoruba) student who courts her (Mama mistakenly calls him Liberian), says her straightened hair is a "mutilation." Beneatha later cuts her hair into a natural style, and Asagai asks her to marry him and practice medicine in Nigeria.

**"Alaiyo"**
The Yoruba nickname that Asagai gives Beneatha. It means "one for whom bread—food—is not enough," reflecting her hunger for identity and meaning.

**"OCOMOGOSIAY!" and "FLAMING SPEAR!"**
Wearing Nigerian robes Asagai gave her, Beneatha dances to African music, chanting "OCOMOGOSIAY," a cry welcoming the men back to the village. Her drunk brother Walter joins in, jumps on the table, shouts "FLAMING SPEAR! HOT DAMN!" and "And Ethiopia stretch forth her hands again!"

**Mama's plant**
Mama tends a small, "feeble little" houseplant on the windowsill that gets little sun but grows "doggedly," comparing it to her children. It symbolizes her dream of a garden and a house. The play ends with her coming back into the empty apartment to take the plant with her. As a moving gift, Travis gives her an oversized gardening hat ("I always wanted me one just like it!").

**Langston Hughes's "Harlem"**
The title comes from Hughes's poem "Harlem," which asks "What happens to a dream deferred? / Does it dry up / like a raisin in the sun?" The poem fits the play's theme of each character's postponed dreams.

**Bruce Norris's Clybourne Park and other adaptations**
Bruce Norris's Pulitzer-winning Clybourne Park (2010) responds to the play. Its first act shows the white couple Bev and Russ selling their house to the Youngers, haunted by the suicide there of their son Kenneth, a Korean War veteran, and it includes Karl Lindner. Kwame Kwei-Armah's Beneatha's Place imagines Beneatha later as a dean of social sciences, and Raisin, a musical by Judd Woldin, won the Tony for Best Musical. Hansberry's writing was supported by royalties from the hit song "Cindy, Oh Cindy."

**Mrs. Johnson**
A gossiping neighbor in a scene often cut from productions. She jokes that, according to the newspaper, "this time next month" the Youngers may be bombed out of their new house, referring to violence against Black families who moved into white neighborhoods.

**"DAMN MY EGGS!"**
In the opening scene, Walter tries to discuss his liquor store plan with Ruth, who answers him by telling him to eat his eggs. After he says he doesn't want his eggs scrambled, she scrambles them, and he complains that women always tell men to eat their eggs, finally shouting "DAMN MY EGGS!" The play opens with Ruth waking Travis and Walter, and Walter tells Travis that he is not the only one who needs to use the shared bathroom.

**Ruth's pregnancy and abortion**
Ruth discovers that she is pregnant and secretly considers an abortion because the family cannot afford another child, putting a five-dollar down payment on one. Mama argues against it, and the phrase "the part that's already living" comes up when they discuss it. The new house gives Ruth hope.

**Beneatha's atheism and medical ambitions**
Beneatha declares that God does not exist and that "there is only man and it is he who makes miracles," and Mama slaps her and makes her repeat "In my mother's house there is still God." Beneatha says she became interested in medicine as a child after watching a boy named Rufus get hurt in a sledding accident. After the money is lost she nearly gives up on becoming a doctor.

**George Murchison**
Beneatha's wealthy, assimilated boyfriend, who dismisses her interest in African heritage. Walter tries to talk "investments" with him and mocks his white shoes, which George calls the "college style." Beneatha rejects George for the more idealistic Asagai, and she mocks Walter's business dreams by calling him "Symbol of a Rising Class" and "Titan of the System."
